title: Heuristics with performance guarantees for the minimum number of matches problem in heat recovery network design
contribution: Nine heuristics with performance guarantees for the strongly NP-hard minimum-number-of-matches MILP in heat exchanger network synthesis: a bin-packing NP-hardness reduction, a big-M-free single-interval MILP, a tight 1.5-approximate greedy, tighter big-M values via a max-heat greedy, tight and new ratios for rounding, water-filling and greedy-packing heuristics, and a released 51-instance study.
problem_entry: Bottleneck MILP of the sequential HENS method; exact solvers fail on moderate instances and big-M relaxations are weak; builds on Furman-Sahinidis approximation algorithms and aims at many good solutions for Floudas's downstream NLP (pp. 1-3, 37).
key_idea: Treat the problem as packing: acyclic optimal solutions give v = n+m-l and a big-M-free bin MILP, equal-load matching gives a 1.5 ratio, max-flow-based MHG tightens big-M, greedy packing selects matches maximising transferable heat (pp. 9-14, 26).
assumptions: Standard transportation/transshipment MILP over temperature intervals; worst-case ratios; equal heat loads admitted to be a thought experiment; Theorem 7 ratio depends on precision epsilon (pp. 3-8, 12, 26).
proof_devices: Lower-bound-then-ratio template shown as a figure (Fig. 2, p. 9)
NP-hardness reduction from bin packing (Thm 1, p. 9; App. A p. 41)
Forest structure of an optimal single-interval solution, v = n+m-l (p. 10; App. B)
Tightness of ratios 2 (SG) and 1.5 (IG) by worst-case instances (Thms 2-3, p. 12; pp. 42-44)
Negative Omega(n) and positive filling-ratio guarantees for LP rounding (Thms 4-5, pp. 17-18)
Max-flow/min-cut correctness of the max-heat greedy MHG (p. 13)
Greedy charging argument with unit costs 1/E_l for the logarithmic LHM-LP ratio (Thm 7, pp. 26, 49-50)
experiments: 51 instances (26 Furman, digitised and released; 10 Chen et al.; 12 Grossmann; 3 random 160-stream) with CPLEX 12.6.3 and Gurobi 6.5.2 as exact baselines, heuristic ratio and CPU box plots, big-M comparison; exact solvers best on literature sets, greedy packing best heuristic, CPLEX untuned (pp. 28-35).
positioning: Extends and re-analyses Furman and Sahinidis (2004): their ratio 2 shown tight, their FLPR, LRR and WFG improved with tighter big-M (pp. 12, 31, 35).
writing: Contribution table separating new from inherited guarantees (Table 2, p. 10); a dedicated contributions-discussion section (pp. 35-37).
limits_future: LHM-LP slow in practice; rounding and water filling trade quality for speed; big-M reduction and fast primal solutions suggested for exact methods (pp. 31, 36-37).

method_links.note: Exploits the problem's packing structure, acyclic optimal solutions and interval residual capacities
New public test set and two exact solvers, but CPLEX deliberately not tuned; concedes exact solvers win on literature instances

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Proves tight worst-case ratios for practitioners' heuristics, then improves them with one structural step

transferable: Re-analyse a published heuristic before replacing it: prove its ratio tight, add one structural step, prove the new ratio tight (p. 12)
Pair a negative worst-case result with a positive parametrised one so the analysis points to the fix (tighter big-M) (pp. 17-18, 35)
Report the exact solver's incumbent over time against the heuristic's fast answer (p. 34)
Aim an upstream step of a sequential decomposition at several provably good solutions for an easy downstream solve (pp. 3, 37)

quotes.text: In practice, hot and cold process streams are unlikely to have equal supplies and demands of heat, so discussing equal heat loads is largely a thought experiment.
the point of this paper is to develop a deep understanding of a very important problem that consistently arises in process systems engineering

title: Design of Experiments for Model Discrimination Hybridising Analytical and Data-Driven Approaches
contribution: Replaces non-analytical rival models with GP surrogates learnt from simulations so that classical analytical design-of-experiments and model-discrimination criteria apply to black-box models, matching the analytical method on a classical case and designing in minutes rather than days.
problem_entry: Regulated healthcare needs interpretable mechanistic models; classical criteria need parameter gradients that legacy ODE/PDE code lacks, Monte Carlo design takes days while experiments take 1-4 days (pp. 1-4).
key_idea: GP surrogate of each model over design and parameter space; first/second-order Taylor marginalisation of parameters on the surrogate mean and variance; reuse Box-Hill, Buzzi-Ferraris and Akaike criteria (pp. 4-5).
assumptions: Gaussian i.i.d. measurement noise with known covariance; Gaussian parameter posterior around the best fit; RBF kernel for smooth ODE outputs; point-estimate GP hyperparameters (pp. 2, 4-5).
proof_devices: No theorems; first- and second-order Taylor expansions of GP mean and variance in theta give closed-form marginal predictive moments (Eqs. 7-16, p. 5)
experiments: Case 1 (4 analytical kinetic models, 500 tests) vs analytical method and uniform random design with success/failure/inconclusive rates; case 2 (ODE biochemical networks) shows an indiscriminable model pair, resolved by removing it (pp. 5-7).
positioning: Positions itself between classical analytical methods (Box-Hill, Buzzi-Ferraris, Michalik) and Monte Carlo Bayesian design (Vanlier, Drovandi, Ryan, Woods) (pp. 3-4).
writing: Opens from regulatory requirements (EMA/FDA) before the method (pp. 1-2); explicit 'Limitations' paragraphs for each prior family (pp. 3-4).
limits_future: Relies on the Gaussian parameter approximation (mixture extension suggested); accuracy traded for tractability; future dual control and other biological model classes (p. 8).

method_links.note: The model is again the object of optimisation, but a black-box mechanistic model is replaced by a differentiable surrogate rather than encoded exactly as constraints
Failure and inconclusive rates reported beside successes, with a random-design control

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: surrogate only the broken ingredient of a classical method
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Gradients unavailable, so a GP surrogate supplies them while the classical criteria are kept

transferable: Report success, failure and inconclusive rates separately for a sequential decision procedure, with a uniform-random baseline (pp. 5-7)
Test an indiscriminability explanation directly by removing the suspect rival and re-running (p. 7)
Substitute only the failed ingredient of a classical method with a learned surrogate so the hybrid can be checked against the classical method on its home ground (pp. 4-5)

quotes.text: For model discrimination, we wish to be agnostic with regards to the software implementation or model type
In practice, researchers faced with apparent model indiscriminability have to rethink their experimental set-up to lower measurement noise or add measured states.

title: Approximation Algorithms for Process Systems Engineering
contribution: Not read: the extracted file is the 2019 arXiv preprint (1909.12328v1, six authors) of the 2020 journal paper S069, not this ESCAPE-28 conference paper.
coauthors: D. Letsios, G. Kouyialis (per the work list)

title: Bayesian multiobjective optimisation with mixed analytical and black-box functions: application to tissue engineering
contribution: Closed-form EHVI and EMmI acquisition functions for Bayesian multiobjective optimisation with one analytical and one GP-modelled black-box objective, outperforming twelve genetic algorithms and random search on test problems and a bone-tissue bioreactor model, and yielding a cost-filling Pareto frontier from an expensive PDE model.
problem_entry: Bioreactor design with an expensive single-machine PDE filling objective and a cheap analytical cost; existing Bayesian MOO treats all objectives as black boxes; re-implementing the legacy model was costed at six person-months (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Model only the black box with a GP, keep the cost deterministic (Dirac delta joint density), and derive closed-form mixed EHVI and EMmI (pp. 5-7).
assumptions: Two objectives, one deterministic; smoothness-encoding GP kernel; black-box evaluation dominates GP and acquisition cost; simplified linear medium-cost model (pp. 3, 5, 11-12).
proof_devices: No theorems; rectangle decomposition of the dominated region for closed-form expected hypervolume improvement (Eqs. 1-2, pp. 5-6)
experiments: ODE model plus five test problems with varied frontier shapes, 12 Platypus GAs at defaults and random search, 10+50 evaluations, 25 repeats, GD/MPFE/log-VR metrics; scaling to D=30; full PDE: 8 historical + 14 EMmI points over two months (pp. 7-11).
positioning: Compares against genetic algorithms as the most common biomedical MOO approach; extends a conference paper on one acquisition function (pp. 2, 9).
writing: States the journal increment over the conference paper in one paragraph (p. 2); discussion names the regime where competitors win (p. 11).
limits_future: GAs and random search win in wall-clock time when surrogate cost exceeds black-box cost; GPs scale poorly with dimension; kernel choice matters (pp. 11-12).

method_links.note: Exploits the known analytical part of the problem instead of treating every objective as a black box
Broad competitor set with repeats and standard errors, but competitors at default parameters and no strengthened baseline; do-not-use regime written in

transferable: Keep cheap, known objectives exact inside the acquisition function and surrogate only the expensive one (p. 5)
Benchmark algorithms on a cheap reduced-order model of the simulator, then spend the expensive budget once with the chosen variant (pp. 7, 10)
Use a log transform of the hypervolume ratio so differences near 100% are visible (p. 8)
coauthors: Simon Olofsson, Mohammad Mehrian, Roberto Calandra, Liesbet Geris, Marc Peter Deisenroth

quotes.text: We could replicate the existing model, but we estimate six person-months for recreating and validating the new code.

However, for problems where training the surrogate model and/or evaluating the posterior predictive distribution is more expensive than evaluating the black-box function, genetic algorithms and random search will be able to explore the variable space much quicker (in terms of wall clock time) than Bayesian optimisation, giving them an advantage.

title: GPdoemd: A Python package for design of experiments for model discrimination
contribution: Adds a closed-form quadratic Jensen-Renyi divergence design criterion, extends the GP-surrogate design-of-experiments method to sparse GPs, and releases GPdoemd, a modular open-source package with switchable kernels, marginalisation schemes, design criteria and discrimination methods plus bundled case studies.
problem_entry: Rival mechanistic models with too little data; classical criteria need gradients, automatic differentiation fails on non-smooth models, Monte Carlo design takes days or weeks (p. 2).
key_idea: Quadratic Renyi entropy gives a closed-form divergence for Gaussian predictive distributions, agnostic to model weighting; GP surrogates supply the predictive distributions for black-box models; seven switchable modules in GPdoemd (pp. 9-10, 19-21).
assumptions: Gaussian noise with known or upper-bounded covariance; Gaussian parameter posterior; fixed 99.9% decision thresholds in the tests, admitted to be high (pp. 3, 21, 34-35).
proof_devices: No theorems; closed-form Gaussian-mixture quadratic Renyi entropy (Eqs. 12-15, pp. 9-10)
Qualitative criterion comparison on constructed predictive distributions with constant, decreasing and increasing variance (Figs 3-5, pp. 10-12)
experiments: Four case studies with 100 random initial sets each; D_JR vs classical criteria vs uniform random design; GP-T1/GP-T2 vs the analytical method framed as not significantly worse; indiscriminable biochemical model removed and re-run (pp. 22-25, 30-32).
positioning: Extends the authors' own conference papers, stating which sections and tables repeat them (p. 3); Jensen-Renyi offered as a closed-form alternative to Vanlier et al.'s Monte Carlo Jensen-Shannon criterion (p. 9).
writing: Explicit scope sentences in the discussion: no training-data guideline, tests not fully representative (pp. 33-34).
limits_future: GP scaling to large training sets; no guideline for training data; future information criteria, global parameter estimation, batch designs, state-space models (pp. 33-35).

method_links.note: Toolkit with rival options as switches (design criteria, discrimination methods) appears in 2019, but over mechanistic models rather than trained ML models
Random-design control, failure and inconclusive rates, written scope paragraph

transferable: When an entropy-based criterion is intractable, switch to an entropy family member with a closed form for your distribution class (pp. 9-10)
Ship the benchmark case studies inside the package so others can compare directly (pp. 19, 36)
When extending a conference paper, state which sections and tables repeat it and which are new (p. 3)
coauthors: Simon Olofsson, Lukas Hebing, Sebastian Niedenfuehr (Bayer AG), Marc Peter Deisenroth

quotes.text: we do not attempt to provide general guidelines for how best to generate training data.
The Section 6 experiments are not in every way representative of model discrimination in a real setting.

title: A multilevel analysis of the Lasserre hierarchy
contribution: Defines primal and dual prolongation operators that map a solution of the order-w Lasserre SDP relaxation to the order w+1, proves feasibility of prolongated points and vanishing duality gap of prolongated optimal points, and uses them as a warm start that speeds SDPT3 by 1.02-1.76x on binary POPs.
problem_entry: Lasserre relaxations grow exponentially with order and lower-level solutions are discarded; links between levels claimed studied for the first time (pp. 1-2, 26).
key_idea: Primal: project first-order moments onto K and lift to monomials; dual: embed coarse matrices as leading principal submatrices padded with zeros; warm-start an infeasible IPM after lifting small eigenvalues (pp. 10-12, 21-22).
assumptions: Compact feasible set with tractable projection (Assumption 1.1, practical not theoretical); unique POP solution for Theorem 4.3, enforced in tests by a small linear perturbation (pp. 3, 14, 18).
proof_devices: Nesting lemma: order-w data matrices are leading principal submatrices of order-(w+1) matrices, new monomials have zero blocks (Lemma 3.1, p. 8)
Primal prolongation of any point is feasible at the fine level (Thm 4.1, p. 11)
Dual residuals carry over unchanged and vanish on new monomials (Thm 4.2, p. 12)
Duality gap of prolongated optima tends to zero via Lasserre convergence and invariance of the dual objective under padding (Thm 4.3, pp. 14-15)
experiments: 800 random binary POPs (quadratic {0,1}, MAX-CUT, integer partition; n=10-20) via SparsePOP; SDPT3, SeDuMi, Mosek at 1e-7; solved-by-level and projection counts, prolongated-point quality, wins and time ratios under normalised stopping; multilevel beats SDPT3 but Mosek up to 10x faster on larger problems (pp. 18-27).
positioning: Builds on Campos and Parpas's multigrid SDP operators and sparse relaxations of Waki et al.; positions against structure-exploiting and first-order SDP methods (pp. 2, 21).
writing: Limits stated in the introduction before any result (pp. 2-3); conclusion opens its claim with an explicit 'we do not claim' (p. 26).
limits_future: Bounded by SDP size and by IPMs' weak use of initial points; prolongated points off the central path; SDPNAL+ showed no gain; Mosek lacks warm start; future newer hierarchies such as BSOS (pp. 2-3, 21, 26, 28).

method_links.note: Works between levels of a hierarchy, but exploits nesting of consecutive levels to reuse a coarse solution rather than building a family between two extremes
Stopping criteria normalised across solvers before timing; loss to Mosek written in with explicit scoping

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: coarse-to-fine reuse of a cheaper relaxation level
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Prolongation operators carry order-w solutions to order w+1 as feasible warm starts; projection of coarse solutions checked first

transferable: Before solving the next relaxation level, check whether projecting the current level's solution already solves the original problem (pp. 19-20)
Compare warm-started and cold solvers by time ratios under one normalised stopping rule (pp. 24-26)
Report a negative preliminary result with another base solver in a footnote with a candidate explanation (p. 21)

quotes.text: Unfortunately, exploiting initial points is a challenging and open problem for interior point algorithms, and this issue sets an upper bound on the performance of the prolongation operators developed in this paper.
we do not claim that the warm start method (which we have referred as the multilevel approach) is better than any other IPM or any other alternative to solve POPs
